questions.question: Which of the following is an unpaired vessel in the central nervous system?
questions.explanation:
The basilar artery and the anterior spinal artery are unpaired arteries in the central nervous
system.

The basilar artery is a single artery formed by the union of two vertebral arteries.
The anterior spinal artery is a single artery formed from a branch from each vertebral artery near
its termination.

questions.question: The chief artery of the superolateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere is:
questions.explanation:
The chief artery of the superolateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere is the middle cerebral
artery.
Both the anterior and middle cerebral artery supply the superolateral surface of the brain but
anterior cerebral artery supplies only a narrow strip at the upper superolateral surface rest is
supplied by the middle cerebral artery. Therefore, the chief artery is the middle cerebral artery.
The chief artery of the medial surface of the brain is an anterior cerebral artery.
The chief artery of the inferior surface of the brain is the posterior cerebral artery”
Lateral cerebral artery is not an artery. ae e.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man was diagnosed with stroke. A thrombus in the marked vessel will affect all of the following structures except:
questions.explanation:
The marked vessel is posterior cerebral artery. It does not supply the pons, hence a thrombus in
this artery will not affect the pons.
The branches of the posterior cerebral artery are:
+ Cortical branches
+ Occipital lobe - visual cortex
+ Temporal lobe - medial and inferolateral surfaces
+ Central branches
+ Thalamus
+ Subthalamus
+ Lentiform nucleus

* Midbrain
+ Pineal gland
+ Superior and inferior colliculi
+ Medial and lateral geniculate bodies
+ Choroidal branches- choroid plexus of
+ Lateral ventricle
+ Third ventricle

questions.question: A patient presents with vertigo, nystagmus, left-sided Horner's syndrome with numbness of left face and right limbs. What is the largest branch of the affected artery marked in the image as 'X'?

suspectLines.text: \ eM 92 A RED eb yra1 acory

questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Wallenberg's syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome)
and the marked vessel is the vertebral artery. The largest branch of this artery is the posterior
inferior cerebellar artery.
The vertebral artery is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. It enters the skull
through the foramen magnum and terminates by joining the vertebral artery of the opposite side
forming the basilar artery. The branches of the cranial portion of the vertebral artery are:
+ Meningeal branches - supplying dura of posterior cranial fossa
+ Posterior spinal arteries - supply posterior one-third of the spinal cord
+ Anterior spinal artery - supply anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord
+ Posterior inferior cerebellar artery - supplies the lateral part of the medulla, cerebellar
hemisphere, and the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle.
+ Medullary branches - supplying the medulla

questions.question: A hypertensive man suffered a sudden, right brachiofacial paresis with dysarthria. CT showed a haemorrhage in the left basal ganglia and angiography revealed a Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm. The affected artery is a branch of:
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm. The affected artery is
the Charcot's artery which is the striate branch of the middle cerebral artery marked as 'C' in the
above image.

Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms are located in the lenticulostriate vessels of the basal ganglia and
are commonly associated with hypertension. Charcot's artery supplies the internal capsule and
basal ganglia. It is also known as the 'Charcot's artery of cerebral haemorrhage'.

questions.explanation:

Heubner is not a part of its blood supply.
The posterior limb of internal capsule is supplied by:
+ Charcot's artery (branch of middle cerebral artery)
+ Anterior choroidal artery (branch of internal carotid artery)

+ Posterolateral branches of posterior cerebral artery.

Superficial veins: > “
+ Superion ie? al veins:
These vein$ drain the upper parts of the superolateral and medial surfaces of the cerebral

+ Inferior cerebral veins:
These veins return blood from the inferior aspect of the cerebral hemisphere into the transverse,

+ Superficial middle cerebral vein:
This vein receives blood from veins on the superolateral surface. It terminates in the cavernous
sinus.
Deep veins:
+ Internal cerebral veins:
This pair of veins originates at the foramen of Munro and eventually anastomoses to form the
great vein of Galen.

+ Basal veins:
The two basal veins are closely related to the midbrain structures and drain into the great vein of
Galen.
+ Great cerebral vein:
The two internal cerebral veins unite to form the great cerebral vein before it passes beneath the
corpus callosum and anastomoses with the straight sinus.
